title: Unlink Every Matching Node
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list and an integer target. Remove every node whose value equals target and return the head of what is left. The other nodes keep their order.

The head itself may need to go, and so may every node; return an empty list in that case.

examples.why: The first, middle and last nodes all hold 4, so the new head is the old second node.
Every node goes. A loop that only fixes the head once leaves a 6 behind.
Two matches in a row. After unlinking the first 3, stay on 1 and check its new next before moving on.

hints: Removing a middle node means pointing its predecessor past it. What is the predecessor of the head?
A dummy node placed before the head gives every real node a predecessor, so the head stops being a special case.
From the dummy, look at cur.next. If it matches, skip it and stay put; otherwise move cur forward.

explain.intuition:
To unlink a node you change the next of the node before it. The head has no node before it, which is the source of most bugs here. Put a dummy node in front, and every real node now has a predecessor.

Then walk with cur, always looking one step ahead. If cur.next matches, splice it out and do not move, because the new cur.next may match too. Only advance when the next node stays.
steps: Create dummy with dummy.next = head and set cur = dummy.
While cur.next exists: if cur.next.val === target, set cur.next = cur.next.next.
pitfalls: Advancing after every removal. With two matches in a row, the second one is skipped over and survives.
Handling the head with a single if. A list that starts with several matches needs a loop, or simply the dummy node.
Returning head instead of dummy.next. If the head was removed, head still points at the removed node.

solutions.title: Collect nodes, relink from the back
solutions.idea: Store the nodes in an array, then walk it backwards: each kept node points at the already-cleaned rest. Simple, but uses O(n) memory.

solutions.title: Dummy node, look one step ahead
solutions.idea: A dummy before the head means every node has a predecessor. Splice out matches without moving; move only past nodes that stay.

followups: Write the recursive version. Why can it overflow the call stack on a long list?
Remove every node whose value appears more than once in the list (list not sorted).
